a16z's Angela Strange sits down with @Valon's Andrew Wang and Linda Du to unpack what it takes to rebuild the infrastructure underneath a $13 trillion mortgage market that still relies heavily on systems designed before the internet.

Linda and Andrew explain why Valon chose the hardest path: becoming a regulated mortgage servicer, translating decades of federal and state regulation into software, and proving the platform on its own loans before selling it to the industry. That foundation made Valon roughly 3x as efficient as traditional servicing and created the system of record it is now using to bring AI into complex mortgage workflows.

They also discuss what AI makes possible on top of that infrastructure, from agents handling long-tail servicing tasks to voice interfaces and more personalized customer experiences. And they explain why deploying the technology into large regulated enterprises is ultimately as much a change-management challenge as a technical one.

Employment Friday delivered a split report: non-farm payrolls came in well below expectations while household employment rose more than 400,000. But Cathie Wood opened this month's episode somewhere unusual, with a tweet from Bill Ackman.

Ackman's argument is that rising interest costs could feed a vicious inflation cycle. Cathie Wood says she first heard that case in the late 1970s, when inflation was stuck in double digits. She believes this period looks far more like the 1980s, when productivity drove real growth up and an early technology revolution drove inflation down.

The 10-year Treasury yield is now above 5%, after dipping below 1% during COVID. Pulling the chart back to 1790, Cathie Wood says 5% sits near the midpoint of American history, though higher than during large stretches of it. In our view, the anomaly was not today, it was the spike from the 1970s through COVID, which she traces to the closing of the gold window in 1971.

Inflation is cooling at the margin. Headline personal consumption expenditures (PCE) inflation was revised down to 3.4% from 3.7%, with core lower still. Truflation's headline reads roughly 2.7%, with oil probably a big part of the recent tick up, while its core keeps ticking down. The diffusion index that Fed (Federal Reserve) Chairman Kevin Warsh watches has reversed quickly, which Cathie Wood calls a very important piece of information.

On the dollar, Cathie Wood pushed back hard on the idea that American exceptionalism is finished. The Fed's real trade-weighted dollar, measured across 26 countries, is not far from all-time highs. She points to data showing 90% of the world's data center financing is happening in the US, and to an effective US corporate tax rate near 8%, the lowest in the world, driven by 100% first-year depreciation.

Artificial intelligence (AI) inference costs are falling 99.99% per year at a fixed performance level. Cathie Wood invokes Jevons paradox: as price collapses, volume explodes. She points to OpenAI going from a $20 billion annualized revenue run rate at the end of last year to $70 billion, against Anthropic's $65 billion reported in July.

That math drives the growth forecast. ARK has been projecting 7.3% real global gross domestic product (GDP) growth over the five years ending 2030, against an International Monetary Fund (IMF) forecast closer to 2.5 to 3%. Cathie Wood says the chart gets updated in January's Big Ideas. She expects productivity growth to accelerate into the 5 to 6% plus range.

On oil, 57% of consumption goes to transportation, and transportation is electrifying. Cathie Wood believes oil could fall into the $30 to $35 range, a level previously reached only during crises. This time she expects a technological shift rather than a crisis to take it there.

The yield curve is the chart she keeps returning to. Steepness never got back to the 200 to 300 basis point (2 to 3%) range through COVID, and where COVID's steepening reached about 150 basis points, this cycle peaked near 75 and now sits in the 40s. Cathie Wood reads that as Treasury yields sniffing out deflationary undercurrents.

On credit, bank credit default swaps show no systemic risk. But the hyperscalers, cash fortresses that avoided the debt markets for years, are tapping them now, and their credit default swaps are deteriorating. Cathie Wood flags that as the unusual development worth watching.

Watch In The Know for @CathieDWood's full economic breakdown. ⬇️
